subject: Historia
title: The Enlightenment and the Revolutions
sourceSummary: How the 1700s' new ideas about reason, freedom and human rights challenged kings and the church, and how the ideas were put into practice in the American and the French Revolutions.
topics: Napoleon and the spread of the ideas

questions.prompt: What did the thinkers of the Enlightenment believe was the most important path to knowledge?
questions.opener: The word "enlightenment" is about shedding light on ignorance – with the help of something every person has.
choices: The traditions of the church and interpretation of the Bible
Reason and one's own capacity for critical thought
The king's commands and laws
Old myths and folk belief
questions.explanation: The Enlightenment philosophers argued that human beings, using their own reason and scientific methods, could understand the world and improve society. Precisely because of this, they questioned whether the church's traditions or the king's will should decide what is true, which makes the options about the church and the king wrong.

questions.prompt: Which thinker is best known for the idea that power should be divided between legislative, executive and judicial power?
questions.opener: This idea is called the separation of powers and comes from a French thinker of the 1700s.
choices: Voltaire
Jean-Jacques Rousseau
John Locke
Montesquieu
questions.explanation: Montesquieu developed the separation of powers in his work "The Spirit of the Laws" (1748): if power is divided up, the different branches can check one another so that no one becomes absolute. Voltaire wrote above all about freedom of speech and religious tolerance, while Rousseau developed the idea of the general will and the social contract.

questions.prompt: What was an important cause of the American colonies rebelling against Britain?
questions.opener: The colonists' slogan was "no taxation without representation".
choices: The colonies were forced to pay new taxes to Britain without having their own representatives in the British parliament
Britain refused to sell goods to the colonies
The colonists wanted to reintroduce monarchy in America
France demanded that the colonies become independent
questions.explanation: After costly wars, Britain imposed new taxes and duties on the colonies, which at the same time had no representatives in parliament in London – the demand for influence became a central cause of the uprising in 1775. The colonists, on the contrary, wanted to be rid of monarchy, and France became an ally only during the war, not the one making the demand.

questions.prompt: In which year was the Bastille in Paris stormed, the event usually counted as the start of the French Revolution?
questions.opener: The date is France's national day: 14 July.
questions.explanation: The Bastille was stormed on 14 July 1789 and became the symbol of the people challenging the king's absolute rule. The year 1776 belongs to the American Declaration of Independence and 1815 to Napoleon's final defeat, both later stages.

questions.prompt: Which three words became the French Revolution's most famous slogan?
questions.opener: They still appear on French public buildings.
choices: King, church and fatherland
Liberty, equality, fraternity
Bread, peace and land
Order, law and obedience
questions.explanation: "Liberté, égalité, fraternité" – liberty, equality, fraternity – summed up the revolution's demands for civil rights and the abolition of the privileges of the estate-based society. "King, church and fatherland" instead expresses exactly the old order that the revolutionaries turned against.

questions.topic: Napoleon and the spread of the ideas
questions.prompt: What happened to Napoleon after the defeat at Waterloo in 1815?
questions.opener: He had to leave Europe for good – for a remote island in the Atlantic.
choices: He was crowned king of France
He fled to the USA and lived there for the rest of his life
He retook power in Paris after a few years
He was taken captive to the island of Saint Helena, where he died in 1821
questions.explanation: After Waterloo, Napoleon was taken as a prisoner to the British island of Saint Helena far out in the Atlantic, where he died in 1821. He could therefore not retake power; his brief return, "the Hundred Days", took place before Waterloo, not after.

questions.prompt: Explain why the French Revolution broke out in exactly 1789.
questions.opener: Weigh together long-term injustices, the state's finances, poor harvests and the new ideas.
questions.answer: The revolution broke out in 1789 because several problems coincided. France was a society of estates in which the nobility and the clergy had privileges and paid almost no taxes, while the third estate – farmers, workers and the bourgeoisie – carried the tax burden. At the same time, the state's finances had been driven into the ground after expensive wars, including support for the American colonists. Crop failure made bread very expensive in exactly these years, creating acute hardship in the cities. The ideas of the Enlightenment had, moreover, given people a language for demanding freedom, equality and the influence of the people. When the king was forced to summon the Estates-General to solve the tax crisis, the third estate seized the chance to demand a new constitution, and when the king responded with the military, the people of Paris responded by storming the Bastille.
steps: Long-term cause: the injustices of the estate-based society, in which the nobility and the church had privileges and the third estate paid the taxes.
Economic cause: the state treasury had been emptied by expensive wars, and the king needed new tax revenue.
Acute cause: crop failure and high bread prices in 1788–1789 meant many in the cities were starving.
Cause in ideas: the Enlightenment's thoughts on rights and rule by the people gave the demands legitimacy.
Triggering event: the Estates-General were summoned, the third estate demanded a constitution, and on 14 July 1789 the Bastille was stormed.

questions.topic: Napoleon and the spread of the ideas
questions.prompt: Summarise the Enlightenment, the revolutions and how the ideas spread onward.
questions.opener: Think ideas, thinkers, two revolutions, Napoleon and long-term consequences.
questions.answer: The Enlightenment was a current of ideas in the 1700s that put reason, science, tolerance and human rights first · Montesquieu: separation of powers between legislative, executive and judicial power · Voltaire: freedom of speech and religious tolerance · Rousseau: the general will and the social contract · Locke: natural rights to life, liberty and property · the American Revolution 1775–1783: taxation without representation, the Declaration of Independence in 1776, the USA gained a constitution with separation of powers · the French Revolution of 1789: causes were the injustices of the estate-based society, the state's debt crisis, crop failure and the ideas of the Enlightenment · the Bastille was stormed on 14 July 1789, the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen was adopted the same year, the monarchy was abolished and the Reign of Terror followed · Napoleon took power in 1799, crowned himself emperor in 1804, waged war across Europe and at the same time spread laws (the Code Napoléon) and ideas · defeated at Waterloo in 1815 and taken to Saint Helena · the ideas spread through books, newspapers, the encyclopedia, salons and war, and gave rise to later demands for constitutions, the right to vote and national freedom.
